MEMORANDUM

TO: Client
FROM: [Firm], Contracts Practice Group
DATE: August 10, 2026
RE: Issues and Risk Assessment — Counterparty Draft Account Control Agreement

==================================================================
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
==================================================================
We have reviewed the counterparty's draft Account Control Agreement (the "Agreement") against (i) our internal playbook on account control agreements, (ii) the executed credit agreement, (iii) the depository bank's standard form, (iv) the account details, and (v) the related correspondence and checklists. Our review identified four material deviations introduced by the counterparty's markup: (1) a silent reduction of the indemnification cap, (2) a conversion of the indemnification basket from a deductible to a tipping basket, (3) new Material Adverse Effect (MAE) carve-outs for regulatory action of the type disclosed on Schedule 3.7, and (4) a new limitation period shortening the survival of core representations in a manner that contradicts Exhibit B's survival matrix. We also identified a fifth issue: the indemnification changes would silently shift retained liabilities identified on Schedule 5.2.

Per the client's controlling instruction (the latest message in the deal correspondence thread), the client will concede the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away item.

Of the four deviations, we recommend: CONCEDE the basket conversion (Deviation 2); REJECT the indemnification cap reduction and restore the firm-standard cap (Deviation 1); REJECT the MAE carve-outs (Deviation 3); and REJECT the survival-period reduction as a walk-away item (Deviation 4). We also recommend express protection of Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities (Issue 5).

==================================================================
II. ANALYSIS OF DEVIATIONS, RISKS, AND RECOMMENDED POSITIONS
==================================================================

DEV 1 — INDEMNIFICATION CAP SILENTLY REDUCED
------------------------------------------------------------------
Section(s) Referenced: Section 4 (Indemnification) of the counterparty draft.

Playbook Requirement: The internal playbook requires the market-standard indemnification cap of $250,000,000, or two hundred percent (200%) of the maximum aggregate principal amount outstanding under the Credit Agreement, whichever is greater, consistent with the depository bank's standard form.

Counterparty Position: The counterparty silently reduced the indemnification cap below the firm-standard level without marking the change as an express negotiation point.

Risk Rating: HIGH.

Exposure Analysis: If the cap is reduced, the Secured Party would be left exposed beyond the capped amount in the event of, for example: (a) the Depository Bank's failure to comply with a valid Entitlement Order, resulting in wrongful disposition of funds held in the Account; (b) the assertion of competing claims to the Account that the Depository Bank fails to communicate to the Secured Party; or (c) erroneous disbursement of Account funds contrary to this Agreement. The exposure delta between the firm-standard cap and the counterparty's proposed cap could represent substantial uninsured risk to the Secured Party, particularly given the balances that may flow through the Account over the life of the credit facility. A reduced cap undermines the fundamental protection the Secured Party obtains from the Account Control Agreement as a perfection and enforcement mechanism.

Recommended Position: REJECT the reduction. Restore the firm-standard indemnification cap of $250,000,000, or 200% of the maximum aggregate principal amount under the Credit Agreement, whichever is greater, in accordance with the internal playbook and the depository bank's standard form. Include the standard carve-outs (including gross negligence, willful misconduct, and failure to comply with instructions) that are non-negotiable per the playbook.

------------------------------------------------------------------
DEV 2 — INDEMNIFICATION BASKET CONVERTED FROM DEDUCTIBLE TO TIPPING BASKET
------------------------------------------------------------------
Section(s) Referenced: Section 4 (Indemnification) of the counterparty draft.

Playbook Requirement: The internal playbook requires that the indemnification basket function as a true deductible: the party seeking indemnification bears all losses below the basket threshold, and only amounts above the threshold are recoverable. A tipping basket, by contrast, allows full recovery once the basket threshold is exceeded — a materially more favorable structure for the indemnified party.

Counterparty Position: The counterparty converted the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket.

Risk Rating: LOW (client has instructed concession).

Exposure Analysis: A tipping basket is generally more favorable to the indemnified party (the Secured Party in this context) because once losses cross the threshold, the indemnifying party bears all losses from the first dollar — including the amount below the threshold. Converting from deductible to tipping actually provides MORE protection to the Secured Party, not less. The client's instruction concedes this change, presumably for commercial or strategic reasons during negotiation.

Recommended Position: CONCEDE per the client's controlling instruction. The internal playbook's preference for a deductible basket is departed from only because the client has expressly directed this concession. Document in the negotiation record that this concession was made at client direction and is limited to the basket structure only.

------------------------------------------------------------------
DEV 3 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT CARVE-OUTS FOR REGULATORY ACTION
------------------------------------------------------------------
Section(s) Referenced: Definition of Material Adverse Effect, as modified in the counterparty draft (intersecting with Schedule 3.7 of the Schedules and Exhibits).

Playbook Requirement: The internal playbook and the executed credit agreement define Material Adverse Effect using the firm-standard formulation, which does not include blanket carve-outs for regulatory inquiries or investigations. The firm-standard MAE definition may include limited, specific carve-outs that were the subject of negotiation in the original credit agreement — but the counterparty's proposed carve-outs are overbroad and would exempt the very regulatory matters disclosed on Schedule 3.7.

Counterparty Position: The counterparty added carve-outs to the MAE definition that exclude regulatory actions of the exact kind at issue in this matter — the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7 of the disclosure schedules.

Schedule 3.7 Context: Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that directly intersect with the counterparty's proposed MAE carve-outs. These inquiries concern matters that could constitute a Material Adverse Effect under the firm-standard definition. The counterparty's carve-outs would effectively immunize consequences arising from these inquiries from triggering an MAE, which would undermine the Secured Party's ability to invoke MAE-based protections (decline to fund, demand repayment, take enforcement action, or assert a default).

Risk Rating: HIGH.

Exposure Analysis: If the MAE carve-outs are accepted, the two pending regulatory inquiries on Schedule 3.7 could develop into material adverse developments (fines, penalties, regulatory orders, loss of licenses, business interruption) without giving the Secured Party the exercise of its MAE-based rights under the Credit Agreement and related documents. This could materially impair the Secured Party's position: the collateral (deposit account balances and proceeds) may be rendered less valuable at the precise moment the Secured Party would need to rely on MAE-based rights. The carve-outs would also set a dangerous precedent for narrowing MAE in future financings.

Recommended Position: REJECT the MAE carve-outs. The firm-standard MAE definition should govern without the overbroad regulatory-action carve-outs. If the counterparty insists, counter with narrowly tailored carve-outs that (i) exclude only specific, enumerated regulatory actions that are not material in the context of the credit facility, and (ii) do not extend to the two pending inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7.

------------------------------------------------------------------
DEV 4 — NEW LIMITATION PERIOD SHORTENING SURVIVAL OF CORE REPRESENTATIONS
------------------------------------------------------------------
Section(s) Referenced: Section on Survival of Representations and Warranties (as modified by the counterparty's new limitation period); contradicted by Exhibit B.

Playbook Requirement: Exhibit B to the Schedules and Exhibits sets the survival matrix for the transaction: general representations survive for the duration of the Credit Agreement plus 90 days; fundamental representations (including due organization, authority, enforceability, and security interest perfection) survive indefinitely. The counterparty's proposed limitation period shortens survival for core representations, directly contradicting Exhibit B.

Counterparty Position: The counterparty introduced a new limitation period that would shorten the survival of the core representations below the Exhibit B periods.

Deal Correspondence Instruction (CONTROLLING): The latest message in the deal correspondence thread explicitly states: "the client will concede the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue." The earlier messages in the thread stated a different priority ordering, but only the latest message controls.

Risk Rating: CRITICAL — WALK-AWAY.

Exposure Analysis: A shortened survival period for core representations would have a profound impact on the Secured Party's rights. If the survival period lapses, the Secured Party would be time-barred from bringing claims for breaches of core representations (e.g., the Debtor's authority to execute the Credit Agreement, the Depository Bank's acknowledgment of control, the validity and perfection of the security interest, the enforceability of the agreement). Given that breach of these core representations typically appears in the context of events that may not manifest until well after closing (insolvency proceedings, collateral challenges, or third-party claims), shortening survival could effectively eliminate the Secured Party's recourse for the most consequential categories of breach. The client has instructed that any survival-period reduction is a walk-away item — the client would rather walk away from the transaction than accept a shortened survival period.

Recommended Position: REJECT the survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue per the client's controlling instruction. Restore the Exhibit B survival matrix in full. If the counterparty will not concede, the client should be prepared to terminate negotiations / not proceed with the transaction.

------------------------------------------------------------------
ISSUE 5 — INDIRECT SHIFT OF SCHEDULE 5.2 RETAINED LIABILITIES
------------------------------------------------------------------
Section(s) Referenced: Schedule 5.2 (Retained Liabilities) in the Schedules and Exhibits; Section 4 (Indemnification) of the counterparty draft.

Playbook Requirement: The internal playbook requires that retained liabilities listed on Schedule 5.2 remain the sole responsibility of the Debtor, consistent with the Credit Agreement and the depository bank's standard form. Indemnification provisions must not inadvertently shift these liabilities to the Secured Party or the Depository Bank.

Counterparty Position: The counterparty's indemnification changes, as described above (Dev 1 and Dev 2), would silently shift retained liabilities from the Debtor to the Secured Party. The changes alter the allocation of risk set forth in Schedule 5.2.

Risk Rating: MEDIUM-HIGH.

Exposure Analysis: Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that were expressly allocated to the Debtor in the transaction documents. If the counterparty's indemnification changes are accepted, the Secured Party could become responsible for losses arising from these retained liabilities without having negotiated for that exposure. This represents both a financial risk (liability for the dollar amount of the retained liabilities) and a reputational risk (departing from the bargained-for allocation of risk in the transaction).

Recommended Position: REJECT any changes that shift Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities. Insert an express provision in the Agreement preserving the Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities as the sole responsibility of the Debtor. Require that the indemnification provisions be neutral as between the Secured Party and the Debtor with respect to all retained liabilities.

IV. ADDITIONAL OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
==================================================================

1. Priority of Controlling Instructions. The deal correspondence thread contains earlier messages with a different priority ordering. Only the latest message controls, and it instructs: (i) concede the basket conversion and (ii) treat any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. All analysis in this memorandum and the accompanying redline reflects this controlling instruction.

2. Interaction of Schedule Exceptions. The scheduled exceptions (Schedule 3.7 and Schedule 5.2) control over general statements in the base materials. Where the counterparty markup touches a representation that is also narrowed by a scheduled exception, both sources must be reconciled against the base materials — as reflected in Dev 3 and Issue 5 above.

3. Filename and Documentation Logistics. All deliverables should be filed in the matter workspace using the requested filenames (aca-redline.docx and issues-risk-memo.docx). Do not adopt counterparty-proposed filenames or logistics for the internal workspace.

4. Walk-Away Contingency. Given the client's walk-away instruction with respect to the survival-period reduction (Dev 4), the deal team should be prepared to hold firm. The client should be consulted if the counterparty's position on survival is non-negotiable, to determine whether to invoke the walk-away. No further concessions beyond those already identified should be offered without client approval.

5. Account Details Conformity. The redline incorporates the account number and related account details from the depository bank's records as required by the executed credit agreement and the depository bank's standard form. Ensure the final agreement accurately reflects the specific account subject to control.

6. Execution and Delivery. After the redline is finalized and all deviations are resolved, coordinate execution of the Agreement in counterparts and confirm delivery to all parties, consistent with the closing checklist.

==================================================================
V. CONCLUSION
==================================================================
We recommend proceeding as follows: (a) concede the basket conversion (Dev 2) per client instruction; (b) reject the reduced indemnification cap and restore the firm-standard cap (Dev 1); (c) reject the MAE carve-outs (Dev 3); (d) reject the survival-period reduction as a walk-away item (Dev 4); and (e) protect the Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities (Issue 5). The accompanying redline (aca-redline.docx) implements each of these recommendations in tracked-changes format.
